steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper on local path planning among pushable obstacles (Navigation Among Movable Obstacles) using deep reinforcement learning. It should motivate the problem, cover the limits of prior work, describe our approach and experiments, and outline the rest of the paper.

steps.text:

  - NAMO = objects can be moved around to free space -> still open problem
  - mirrors human instinct: shift furniture / objects blocking the way in densely furnished areas
  - robots could optimize routes by strategically moving obstacles to clear path to destination
- Applications
  - regular maintenance in factories: unused containers, boxes blocking access points
  - domestic service robots, furniture-cluttered homes
  - inspection robots in subterranean environments, rocks and debris
  - effective obstacle manipulation -> greater navigation efficiency
- Prior work + limits
  - NP-hard even in simplified versions (cite)
  - global planning among movable obstacles: iterative and recursive algorithms (cite)
  - simplifications: prior knowledge of environment; offline planning, exponential in number of local obstacles (cite); only axial-aligned pushes
  - local planning with movable objects: minimally studied; few consider sensor inaccuracies / unexpected object dynamics (cite)
  - mostly traditional optimization -> intensive fine tuning, handcrafted design choices
- Our approach
  - deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), Fig. 1
  - neural network, policy-based RL, online agent completes local path plans
  - no axis-aligned pushing constraint; allows uncertainties in sensor inputs and obstacle dynamics
  - targets keyhole problem (cite): go from one disjointed area to another by pushing obstacles through narrow passages
  - pulling / lifting need extra mechanisms (arms); pushing alone still NP-Complete
  - local planner to integrate with global navigation, e.g. A* (cite)
  - Advantage Actor-Critic (cite); NVIDIA Isaac Gym physics engine (cite), parallel agents
- Results
  - familiar environments with new movable obstacle placements
  - entirely unknown environments, unseen movable obstacles
  - real experiments: Unitree Go1 quadruped; sensor inaccuracies, varying real-world obstacle dynamics
- Organization
  - Sec. II literature on NAMO
  - Sec. III problem formulation in RL setting, training in simulation
  - Sec. IV results in simulation and real robot
  - Sec. V conclusion, future directions for NAMO with RL

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In the past decade mobile robots have become very capable, and they can now navigate autonomously in an efficient and safe way even in clutter environments, by avoiding obstacles that are static or that are moving dynamically. However the navigation problem where objects can be moved around to free space, which is also known as Navigation Among Movable Obstacle (NAMO), is still an open problem. The idea is similar to the human instinct to shift furniture or other objects that are blocking their way in densely furnished areas, and it suggests that robots could also optimize their routes by moving obstacles strategically to clear a path to their destination.

This is very relevant for robotics in several scenarios. For example there are tasks with regular maintenance in factories where unused containers and boxes might block access points, there are domestic service robots that navigate through homes cluttered with furniture, and there are robots that do inspections in subterranean environments that are obstructed by rocks and debris. In these settings, being able to manipulate obstacles effectively can greatly improve the efficiency of autonomous navigation.

The problem of moving movable objects around is proved to be NP-hard, even in simplified versions. Previous studies have looked at iterative and recursive algorithms to solve global path planning among movable obstacles, but they often rely on some simplifications. These include having prior knowledge about the environment, planning tasks offline which is exponential to the number of local obstacles, and only allowing axial-aligned object pushes. Local path planning with movable objects on the other hand has been minimally studied in the past. Only a few works consider sensor inaccuracies when dealing with unexpected object dynamics, and they are usually based on traditional optimization methods, which need a lot of fine tuning and handcrafted design choices.

- Our approach
  - DRL (Fig. 1): neural network, policy-based RL, online agent completes local path plans
  - no axis-aligned pushing constraint; uncertainties in sensor inputs and obstacle dynamics allowed
  - keyhole problem: one disjointed area to another, pushing obstacles through narrow passages
  - pulling / lifting need arms etc.; pushing alone still NP-Complete
  - local planner, can plug into global methods like A*
  - Advantage Actor-Critic; NVIDIA Isaac Gym, parallel agents
- Results
  - familiar environments with new obstacle placements; entirely unknown environments, unseen obstacles
  - Unitree Go1 quadruped: sensor inaccuracies, real-world obstacle dynamics
- Organization
  - Sec. II literature; Sec. III formulation + training in simulation; Sec. IV results (sim + real); Sec. V conclusion, future directions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In the past decade mobile robots have become very capable, and they can now navigate autonomously in an efficient and safe way even in clutter environments, by avoiding obstacles that are static or that are moving dynamically. However the navigation problem where objects can be moved around to free space, which is also known as Navigation Among Movable Obstacle (NAMO), is still an open problem. The idea is similar to the human instinct to shift furniture or other objects that are blocking their way in densely furnished areas, and it suggests that robots could also optimize their routes by moving obstacles strategically to clear a path to their destination.

This is very relevant for robotics in several scenarios. For example there are tasks with regular maintenance in factories where unused containers and boxes might block access points, there are domestic service robots that navigate through homes cluttered with furniture, and there are robots that do inspections in subterranean environments that are obstructed by rocks and debris. In these settings, being able to manipulate obstacles effectively can greatly improve the efficiency of autonomous navigation.

The problem of moving movable objects around is proved to be NP-hard, even in simplified versions. Previous studies have looked at iterative and recursive algorithms to solve global path planning among movable obstacles, but they often rely on some simplifications. These include having prior knowledge about the environment, planning tasks offline which is exponential to the number of local obstacles, and only allowing axial-aligned object pushes. Local path planning with movable objects on the other hand has been minimally studied in the past. Only a few works consider sensor inaccuracies when dealing with unexpected object dynamics, and they are usually based on traditional optimization methods, which need a lot of fine tuning and handcrafted design choices.

In this paper we propose a novel approach that uses deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to overcome these limitations, as shown in Fig. 1. We use a neural network for policy-based RL so that an online agent can complete local path plans. Unlike previous work it does not have the constraint of axis-aligned pushing, and it also allows uncertainties in sensor inputs and in obstacle dynamics. Our solution targets the keyhole problem. In this problem a mobile robot wants to go from one disjointed area to another one by pushing obstacles through narrow passages. There are other forms of object manipulation such as pulling or lifting, but they need additional robotic mechanisms such as arms, and just pushing is still NP-Complete. The trained policy is meant for local path planning, and it can be integrated into other global navigation methods such as A*. The approach is based on Advantage Actor-Critic, and we use the NVIDIA Isaac Gym physics engine to simulate and train parallel agents. We show results for policies that can navigate both familiar environments with new placements of movable obstacles and completely unknown environments with movable obstacles they have not seen. We also validate the results with real experiments on a Unitree Go1 quadruped robot, which shows that the policy works with sensor inaccuracies and with the varying dynamics of real obstacles.

The rest of the paper is as follows. Sec. II discusses the literature on the NAMO problem. Sec. III gives the problem formulation in the reinforcement setting and how we implement the training in simulation. Sec. IV presents the results in simulation and in real robot experiments. Sec. V concludes the paper and points to future directions for solving NAMO with RL.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Mobile robots have gained great capabilities in the past decade, so that they can now navigate autonomously, efficiently and safely even in clutter environments by avoiding static or dynamically moving obstacles [1]. However, the navigation problem where objects can be moved around to free space –also known as Navigation Among Movable Obstacle (NAMO)– is still an open problem. This concept mirrors the human instinct to shift furniture or other objects blocking their way in densely furnished areas, and suggests that robots could similarly optimize their routes by strategically moving obstacles to clear a path to their destination. The applications in robotics are relevant in several scenarios, including regular maintenance tasks in factories where unused containers and boxes might block access points, domestic service robots navigating through furniture-cluttered homes, or robots conducting inspections in subterranean environments obstructed by rocks and debris. Effective obstacle manipulation can greatly enhance autonomous navigation efficiency in these settings.

The problem when movable objects need to be moved around is proved to be NP-hard, even in simplified versions [2]. To solve global path planning among movable obstacles, previous studies have explored iterative and recursive algorithms [3], but they often rely on simplifications such as prior knowledge about the environment, offline planning which is exponential to the number of local obstacles [4], and movements limited to axial-aligned object pushes. Local path planning in a movable object setting, on the other hand, has been minimally studied, with only a few works considering sensor inaccuracies when dealing with unexpected object dynamics [5,6,7]; these are usually based on traditional optimization methods that require intensive fine tuning and handcrafted design choices.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to overcome these limitations by employing deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), as depicted in Fig. 1. In particular, we use a neural network for policy-based RL to allow an online agent to complete local path plans without the axis-aligned pushing constraint of previous work, while also allowing uncertainties in sensor inputs and obstacle dynamics. Our solution targets the keyhole problem [8], where a mobile robot aims to traverse from one disjointed area to another by pushing obstacles through narrow passages. We acknowledge that other forms of object manipulation exist, such as pulling or lifting, but these need additional robotic mechanisms such as arms, while just pushing remains NP-Complete. The trained policy is intended for local path planning that can be integrated into other global navigation methods, such as A* [9]. Our approach is based on Advantage Actor-Critic [10] and uses the NVIDIA Isaac Gym physics engine [11] for simulating and training parallel agents. We show outcomes for policies that can navigate both familiar environments with new movable obstacle placements and entirely unknown environments with unseen movable obstacles. Moreover, we validate our findings through real experiments with a Unitree Go1 quadruped robot, showing that the policy is effective in dealing with sensor inaccuracies and varying dynamics of real-world obstacles.

In Sec. II, we discuss the literature on the NAMO problem, and in Sec. III we state the problem formulation in the reinforcement setting and how we implement training in simulation. Sec. IV presents our results both in simulation and with real robot experiments. Finally, Sec. V concludes the paper and points to future directions for solving NAMO with RL.

References:
[1] K. Cai, C. Wang, J. Cheng, C. W. De Silva, and M. Q.-H. Meng, “Mobile Robot Path Planning in Dynamic Environments: A Survey,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2006.14195 , 2020.

[6] J. Scholz, N. Jindal, M. Levihn, C. L. Isbell, and H. I. Christensen, “Navigation Among Movable Obstacles with Learned Dynamic Constraints,” in IEEE/RSJ IROS , 2016, pp. 3706–3713.
